details:
**Chang'e and Hou Yi**
The Chinese moon goddess. Her husband, the archer Hou Yi, shot down nine of the ten suns and received an elixir of immortality from the Queen Mother of the West; Chang'e drank it (in some versions to keep it from the thief Feng Meng) and floated up to the moon, where she lives in the Guanghan Palace. She is honored at the Mid-Autumn Festival, when mooncakes are eaten, and in Journey to the West, Zhu Bajie is banished from heaven for flirting with her.

**Jade Rabbit**
The rabbit that lives on the moon as Chang'e's companion, pounding the elixir of immortality (or, in Japan and Korea, rice cakes) with a mortar and pestle. China's Yutu lunar rover was named after it.

**Selene and Endymion**
Selene, the Greek Titan goddess of the moon, is a daughter of Hyperion and sister of Helios and Eos, and she drives a chariot across the night sky. She fell in love with the shepherd Endymion, who was granted eternal sleep and youth, and in some accounts she bore him fifty daughters. Her Roman counterpart is Luna.

**Tsukuyomi**
The Shinto moon god, born when Izanagi washed his right eye after returning from the underworld, alongside his siblings Amaterasu and Susanoo. He killed the food goddess Ukemochi in disgust because she produced food from her mouth and body, and his angry sister Amaterasu refused to see him again, which is why the sun and moon are separated.

**Coyolxauhqui and Huitzilopochtli**
The Aztec moon goddess who led her four hundred brothers in an attack on their mother Coatlicue. The newly born war god Huitzilopochtli killed her, cutting off her head and throwing it into the sky, where it became the moon.

**Thoth and Khonsu's five extra days**
Ra had forbidden the sky goddess Nut to give birth on any day of the year. Thoth gambled with the moon god Khonsu and won enough of the moon's light to create five extra days, on which Nut bore Osiris, Horus the Elder, Set, Isis, and Nephthys. Thoth himself, depicted as an ibis or baboon, was also a lunar god.

**Tecciztecatl and the rabbit**
In the Aztec creation of the Fifth Sun at Teotihuacan, the proud god Tecciztecatl hesitated out of fear before leaping into the sacrificial fire after Nanahuatzin. Both became suns, so the gods threw a rabbit in Tecciztecatl's face to dim him, creating the moon and its rabbit-shaped markings. He is often identified with the moon god Metztli and depicted with a seashell on his back.

**Mani and Hati**
Mani is the Norse personification of the moon and brother of Sol, the sun. He took the children Hjuki and Bil up from the earth to follow him, and he is chased by the wolf Hati, who will devour him at Ragnarok.

**Nanna and Sin**
The Mesopotamian moon god, called Nanna by the Sumerians and Sin by the Akkadians and Babylonians. He is the son of Enlil and husband of Ningal, his sacred city was Ur, and he is described as having a beard of lapis lazuli.

**Mama Quilla**
The Inca moon goddess, wife (and sister) of the sun god Inti. She was said to weep tears of silver and was associated with the calendar and with women.

**Artemis**
The Greek goddess of the hunt, also identified with the moon. Her brother Apollo tricked her into shooting Orion, she had Actaeon torn apart after he saw her bathing, and in one account she helped her mother Leto deliver her twin Apollo.

**Self-sacrificing hare**
In a Buddhist Jataka tale, a hare with no food to offer a hungry beggar threw itself into a fire to feed him; the beggar (the god Sakra) placed its image on the moon. In an Aztec version, Quetzalcoatl imprints a rabbit on the moon after it offers itself as food.

**Wu Gang and the osmanthus tree**
A Chinese woodcutter banished to the moon as punishment and forced to chop down a self-healing osmanthus (cassia) tree forever, since every cut closes up again.

**Tale of the Bamboo Cutter**
A Japanese folktale in which an old bamboo cutter finds a tiny girl, Princess Kaguya, inside a bamboo stalk, after which he finds gold in other stalks. She is really from the Capital of the Moon and eventually returns there, and the grieving emperor orders her letter and the elixir she left him burned on the highest mountain, Mount Fuji.

**Ganesha and Chandra**
In Hindu myth, the moon god Chandra laughed at Ganesha when he fell after a feast. Ganesha broke off one of his tusks, threw it at the moon, and cursed him, explaining the moon's waxing and waning.
